issues.explanation: 'Kids crying' is not impossible as a trigger after sexual assault, but with the rest of this profile it lacks a clear thematic link to the assault, threat beliefs, or memory content; compared with the other highly assault-congruent triggers (touch, loss of autonomy), this item is clinically weakly connected and may be incoherent for this same formulation.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Heavy Makeup: heavy make-up
issues.explanation: 'Heavy make-up' is difficult to reconcile with this patient's demographics (57-year-old male) and trauma presentation unless there is specific context not provided. It stands out as the clearest demographic/item mismatch in the five target components.

issues.item: Memory: Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.
issues.explanation: 'I can talk about what happened very easily' conflicts with the rest of the memory profile and overall severe PTSD presentation: it sits awkwardly alongside vivid but fragmented trauma memory and strong threat/appraisal activation after sexual assault. This is a within-node tension, because easy verbal access to the trauma is hard to square with marked fragmentation and severe re-experiencing-linked formulation here.

vignette:
Daniel, a 57-year-old single North American man who worked as a tutor, came to therapy after years of trying to keep his world small enough to feel manageable. He described the assault in a way that was at once detailed and fractured: a man had cornered him after a tutoring session, close enough that Daniel could feel the pressure of another body and the loss of any route out, and he remembered being physically forced to do things he did not choose. What stayed with him most was the touch itself and the humiliating sense that his own body had not responded the way he expected it to. Even now, Daniel could summon vivid images of the room, the angle of the light, the man's hands, and the sound of his own breathing, yet he also said it felt as if parts of the event had been ripped away, leaving missing pieces he could not account for. He would start to tell the story and then stop, saying he knew what happened but could not find words for it. From the beginning, the memories and the bodily reminders were bound together: when someone brushed past him in a hallway or reached out to shake his hand, the scene returned in sharp detail, and with it the sense that he was once again trapped in that moment. Those reminders made him feel isolated and set apart from other people, as if something had happened to him that made him fundamentally different, and he became convinced that his body could no longer be trusted and that he had to be especially careful because you never knew what could happen next.

Over time, those convictions shaped how Daniel moved through ordinary life. He watched other people closely for signs that they might harm him, reading faces and hands and body posture with a kind of urgency that left him exhausted. He chose seats in coffee shops, tutoring centers, and waiting rooms based on which ones gave him the best view of a door or the most protected corner, and he avoided unfamiliar places because he felt unable to assess danger there. The smallest cue could set the whole system in motion: if a man stood too near him on the bus or in the grocery line, Daniel's attention narrowed, and the old images returned with startling clarity. He found himself thinking again of the assault in vivid, sensory fragments, and that memory made the surroundings feel dangerous in a way they had not a moment before. The clearer the memory became, the more certain he felt that something like that could happen again, and that certainty tightened his isolation and his sense that he had to remain on guard. He came to believe that being alone with men was especially risky, and that physical touch, even a brief accidental contact, was not benign but a sign that he might be overpowered. Those reactions fed into his daily habits: he avoided any form of physical contact with others, kept conversations brief, and turned down situations that might bring strong emotions, because feeling too much seemed to open the door to losing control. He also smoked more when his vigilance rose, using it to settle himself after scanning a room or replaying a moment that had unsettled him.

Daniel's avoidance gradually narrowed both his work and his relationships. As a tutor, he began arranging sessions in familiar places and limiting who he met, preferring students and settings he already knew because unfamiliar environments felt unsafe. If he had to wait in a lobby or classroom, he would immediately look for the safest seat and position himself where no one could come up behind him. When a student or colleague offered a handshake, he would step back and make a joke or pretend not to notice, then spend the rest of the interaction watching closely for any sign of threat. The more he tried not to feel, the more the memories intruded in brief, wordless flashes, and the harder it became for him to speak about what had happened without drifting into silence. He described feeling set apart from other people, as though the assault had made him less like everyone else and more exposed to whatever might happen next. By the time he sought help, Daniel was no longer simply trying to get through a bad memory; he was living around it. He had come because the vigilance was wearing him down, the avoidance was shrinking his life, and he was afraid that if he did not find a way to feel safe in his own body again, he would end up cut off from everyone.
